claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figures 1C-F.

claims.claim: Paternal deprivation did not affect total distance covered in the open field test in female mandarin voles.
claims.source: However, the total distance covered by voles the from PC group was not different than that covered by voles in the PD group (Figure 1C–F, Figure 1—source data 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figures 1C-F.

claims.claim: Biparental care male voles spent more time in the light compartment than paternal deprivation male voles in the light and dark test.
claims.source: In the light and dark test, PC voles spent more time in the light compartment than did PD voles (male: t(12) = 2.635, p<0.05, Figure 1G and I, Figure 1—source data 1
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data presented in Figures 1G and I.

claims.claim: Biparental care female voles spent more time in the light compartment than paternal deprivation female voles in the light and dark test.
claims.source: In the light and dark test, PC voles spent more time in the light compartment than did PD voles (male: t(12) = 2.635, p<0.05, Figure 1G and I, Figure 1—source data 1; female: t(12) = 3.937, p<0.01, Figure 1H and J, Figure 1—source data 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data presented in Figures 1H and J.

claims.claim: Males in the biparental care group engaged in more investigations of the social stimulus than of the object stimulus.
claims.source: The males of the PC group engaged in more investigations of the social stimulus than of the object stimulus (p<0.025) (Figure 1K, Figure 1—source data 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data presented in Figure 1K.

claims.claim: Preweaning paternal deprivation caused a decrease in social investigations by males during the social preference test.
claims.source: Preweaning PD caused a decrease in social investigations by males during the social preference test (p<0.025) (Figure 1K, Figure 1—source data 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data presented in Figure 1K.

claims.claim: Biparental care group females engaged in more investigations of the social stimulus than of the object stimulus.
claims.source: No significant treatment x stimulus interaction was found on the percentage of investigation time in females (F(1,24) = 1.553, p=0.225), but a main effect of the absence/presence of a social stimulus on mandarin voles was found (F(1,24) = 11.785, p<0.01), such that PC group females engaged in more investigations of the social stimulus than of the object stimulus (p<0.025) (Figure 1L, Figure 1—source data 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data presented in Figure 1L.

claims.claim: Biparental care voles had an increased percentage of c-fos/OT-labeled cells in the PVN after approaching a juvenile vole compared to approaching a toy in males.
claims.source: The post-hoc test indicated that PC voles had an increased percentage of c-fos/OT-labeled cells after approaching a juvenile vole compared to approaching a toy (in both males (p<0.01) (Figure 2E, Figure 2—source data 1)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data presented in Figure 2E.

claims.claim: Biparental care voles had an increased percentage of c-fos/OT-labeled cells in the PVN after approaching a juvenile vole compared to approaching a toy in females.
claims.source: The post-hoc test indicated that PC voles had an increased percentage of c-fos/OT-labeled cells after approaching a juvenile vole compared to approaching a toy (in both males (p<0.01) (Figure 2E, Figure 2—source data 1) and females (p<0.01) (Figure 2F, Figure 2—source data 1)).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data presented in Figure 2F.

claims.claim: Preweaning paternal deprivation reduced the percentage of c-fos/OT-labeled neurons in the PVN after approaching a juvenile vole in females.
claims.source: Preweaning PD only reduced the percentage of c-fos/OT-labeled neurons after approaching a juvenile vole in females (p<0.01) (Figure 2F, Figure 2—source data 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data presented in Figure 2F.

claims.claim: The biparental care group had more positive c-fos-labeled neurons in the prelimbic cortex after exposure to a juvenile vole than after exposure to a toy in males.
claims.source: The PC group had more positive c-fos-labeled neurons after exposure to a juvenile vole than after to exposure to a toy in both males (p<0.01) (Figure 3D, Figure 3—source data 1)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data presented in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: The biparental care group had more positive c-fos-labeled neurons in the prelimbic cortex after exposure to a juvenile vole than after exposure to a toy in females.
claims.source: The PC group had more positive c-fos-labeled neurons after exposure to a juvenile vole than after to exposure to a toy in both males (p<0.01) (Figure 3D, Figure 3—source data 1) and females (p<0.01) (Figure 3E, Figure 3—source data 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data presented in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: The paternal deprivation group had reduced c-fos expression in the prelimbic cortex in males compared to the biparental care group.
claims.source: When compared to the PC group, the PD group also had reduced c-fos expression in males (p<0.01) (Figure 3D, Figure 3—source data 1)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data presented in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: The paternal deprivation group had reduced c-fos expression in the prelimbic cortex in females compared to the biparental care group.
claims.source: When compared to the PC group, the PD group also had reduced c-fos expression in males (p<0.01) (Figure 3D, Figure 3—source data 1) and females (p<0.01) (Figure 3E, Figure 3—source data 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data presented in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: After exposure to a juvenile vole, paternal deprivation males exhibited decreased c-fos expression in the NAc shell when compared with biparental care males.
claims.source: After exposure to a juvenile vole, PD males exhibited decreased c-fos expression in the NAc shell when compared with PC males (p<0.05) (Figure 3F, Figure 3—source data 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data presented in Figure 3F.

claims.claim: Biparental care females exhibited significantly fewer c-fos-positive nuclei in the NAc shell after approaching a juvenile vole than after approaching a toy.
claims.source: PC females exhibited signiﬁcantly fewer c-fos-positive nuclei in the NAc shell after approaching a juvenile vole than after approaching a toy (p<0.01), but c-fos expression in neurons was not affected in PD females (Figure 3G, Figure 3—source data 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data presented in Figure 3G.

claims.claim: Males and females in the paternal deprivation group had fewer PVN OT-IR neurons than males and females in the biparental care group.
claims.source: The results of post-hoc tests indicated that males and females in the PD group had fewer PVN OT-IR neurons than males and females in the PC group (both p<0.01) (Figure 4F, Figure 4—source data 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data presented in Figure 4F.

claims.claim: Females had more PVN OT-IR neurons than males.
claims.source: Females had more PVN OT-IR neurons (p<0.01) than males (Figure 4F, Figure 4—source data 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data presented in Figure 4F.

claims.claim: Paternal deprivation-group males had lower levels of oxytocin receptor protein in the medial prefrontal cortex than biparental care-group males.
claims.source: PD-group males had lower levels of OTR (t(10) = 3.813, p<0.01) (Figure 5A, Figure 5—source data 1)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data presented in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: Paternal deprivation-group males had lower levels of vasopressin 1a receptor protein in the medial prefrontal cortex than biparental care-group males.
claims.source: PD-group males had lower levels of OTR (t(10) = 3.813, p<0.01) (Figure 5A, Figure 5—source data 1) and V1aR (t(10) = 2.375, p<0.05) (Figure 5C, Figure 5—source data 1) proteins in the mPFC than PC-group males.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data presented in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: Paternal deprivation-group females had lower levels of the oxytocin receptor protein in the medial prefrontal cortex than biparental care-group females.
claims.source: PD-group females had lower levels of the OTR protein in the mPFC than PC-group females (t(10) = 4.315, p<0.01) but not in the NAc or PVN (Figure 5B, Figure 5—source data 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data presented in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: Microinjection of oxytocin into the prelimbic cortex increased the percentage of time spent in the central area by males exposed to preweaning paternal deprivation.
claims.source: One-way ANOVA showed that microinjection of OT into the PrL increased the percentage of time spent in the central area by males (p<0.05) and females (1 ng: p<0.05 and 10 ng: p<0.05) that had been exposed to preweaning PD, whereas OT plus either dose of OTA had no effect (except for males injected with 10 ng OT/10 ng OTA, p<0.05).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data presented in Figure 6E.

claims.claim: Microinjection of oxytocin into the prelimbic cortex increased the percentage of time spent in the central area by females exposed to preweaning paternal deprivation.
claims.source: One-way ANOVA showed that microinjection of OT into the PrL increased the percentage of time spent in the central area by males (p<0.05) and females (1 ng: p<0.05 and 10 ng: p<0.05) that had been exposed to preweaning PD, whereas OT plus either dose of OTA had no effect (except for males injected with 10 ng OT/10 ng OTA, p<0.05).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data presented in Figure 6H.

claims.claim: Oxytocin-treated males (10 ng) demonstrated a preference for the social stimulus over the object stimulus.
claims.source: OT-treated males (10 ng) and females (1 ng and 10 ng) demonstrated a preference for the social stimulus over the object stimulus (p<0.008), whereas subjects treated with OT plus either dose of OTA showed no preference (except for males receiving 10 ng OT/10 ng OTA, p<0.008).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data presented in Figure 6G.

claims.claim: Oxytocin-treated females (1 ng and 10 ng) demonstrated a preference for the social stimulus over the object stimulus.
claims.source: OT-treated males (10 ng) and females (1 ng and 10 ng) demonstrated a preference for the social stimulus over the object stimulus (p<0.008), whereas subjects treated with OT plus either dose of OTA showed no preference (except for males receiving 10 ng OT/10 ng OTA, p<0.008).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data presented in Figure 6J.

claims.claim: The majority of neurons expressing ChR2-mCherry coexpressed oxytocin neurons in males (60.6%).
claims.source: The majority of neurons expressing ChR2-mCherry coexpressed OT neurons (male – 132/218 = 60.6%, from two voles; female – 190/268 = 70.9%, from two voles).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of colocalization data from two male voles.

claims.claim: The majority of neurons expressing ChR2-mCherry coexpressed oxytocin neurons in females (70.9%).
claims.source: The majority of neurons expressing ChR2-mCherry coexpressed OT neurons (male – 132/218 = 60.6%, from two voles; female – 190/268 = 70.9%, from two voles).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of colocalization data from two female voles.

claims.claim: Both male and female ChR2-expressing voles showed significantly increased c-fos expression in the prelimbic cortex when compared to control subjects.
claims.source: Both male (Figure 7H, Figure 7—source data 1) and female (Figure 7I, Figure 7—source data 1) ChR2-expressing voles showed signiﬁcantly increased c-fos expression in the PrL when compared to control subjects (p<0.01).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data presented in Figures 7H and 7I.

claims.claim: Optogenetically activated PVN OT neuron terminals in the prelimbic cortex of ChR2-expressing paternal deprivation males induced more investigations of the social stimulus than of the object stimulus.
claims.source: However, a main effect of the absence/presence of a stimulus mandarin vole was found (F(1,20) = 13.350, p<0.01), such that optogenetically activated PVN OT neuron terminals in the PrL of ChR2-expressing PD males induced more investigations of the social stimulus than of the object stimulus (p<0.025).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data presented in Figure 7J.

claims.claim: ChR2-expressing female voles engaged in more investigations of the social stimulus than the object stimulus.
claims.source: ChR2-expressing voles engaged in more investigations of the social stimulus than the object stimulus in males (p<0.025).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data presented in Figure 7K.

claims.claim: Optogenetically activated PVN-PrL OT projections improved the emotions of ChR2-expressing male voles.
claims.source: On the open field test (OFT), optogenetically activated PVN-PrL OT projections improved the emotions of ChR2-expressing voles (male: t(10) = 4.452, p<0.01, Figure 7L, Figure 7—source data 1
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data presented in Figure 7L.

claims.claim: Optogenetically activated PVN-PrL OT projections improved the emotions of ChR2-expressing female voles.
claims.source: On the open field test (OFT), optogenetically activated PVN-PrL OT projections improved the emotions of ChR2-expressing voles (male: t(10) = 4.452, p<0.01, Figure 7L, Figure 7—source data 1; female: t(10) = 4.051, p<0.01, Figure 7M, Figure 7—source data 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data presented in Figure 7M.

claims.claim: Approximately 70.1% of eNpHR3.0-mCherry+ neurons in males overlapped with oxytocin neurons.
claims.source: We also found that approximately 70.1% of eNpHR3.0-mCherry+ neurons in males (471/612, from two voles) or 77.6% of eNpHR3.0-mCherry+ neurons in females (594/765, from two voles) overlapped with OT neurons (Figure 8C and D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of colocalization data from two male voles.

claims.claim: Approximately 77.6% of eNpHR3.0-mCherry+ neurons in females overlapped with oxytocin neurons.
claims.source: We also found that approximately 70.1% of eNpHR3.0-mCherry+ neurons in males (471/612, from two voles) or 77.6% of eNpHR3.0-mCherry+ neurons in females (594/765, from two voles) overlapped with OT neurons (Figure 8C and D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of colocalization data from two female voles.

claims.claim: eNpHR3.0-expressing voles had significantly less c-fos expression than mCherry+ subjects in the prelimbic cortex of males.
claims.source: A histological analysis showed that eNpHR3.0-expressing voles had signiﬁcantly less c-fos expression than mCherry+ subjects in the PrL of males (p<0.01) (Figure 8H, Figure 8—source data 1)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data presented in Figure 8H.

claims.claim: eNpHR3.0-expressing voles had significantly less c-fos expression than mCherry+ subjects in the prelimbic cortex of females.
claims.source: A histological analysis showed that eNpHR3.0-expressing voles had signiﬁcantly less c-fos expression than mCherry+ subjects in the PrL of males (p<0.01) (Figure 8H, Figure 8—source data 1) and females (p<0.01) (Figure 8I, Figure 8—source data 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data presented in Figure 8I.

claims.claim: Both male and female control voles engaged in more investigations of the social stimulus than the object stimulus.
claims.source: Both male and female control voles engaged in more investigations of the social stimulus than the object stimulus (males: p=0.017; females: p<0.01).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data presented in Figures 8J and 8K.

claims.claim: Terminal inhibition of oxytocin neurons projecting from the PVN to the prelimbic cortex attenuated social preference in males.
claims.source: By contrast, terminal inhibition of OT neurons projecting from the PVN to the PrL attenuated social preference in males (Figure 8J, Figure 8—source data 1)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 8J.

claims.claim: Terminal inhibition of oxytocin neurons projecting from the PVN to the prelimbic cortex attenuated social preference in females.
claims.source: By contrast, terminal inhibition of OT neurons projecting from the PVN to the PrL attenuated social preference in males (Figure 8J, Figure 8—source data 1) and females (Figure 8K, Figure 8—source data 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 8K.

claims.claim: Optogenetic inhibition of PVN (OTergic) to the prelimbic cortex pathway significantly increased anxiety-like behavior in males.
claims.source: Optogenetic inhibition of PVN (OTergic) to the PrL pathway significantly increased anxiety-like behavior (males: t(10) = 3.051, p<0.05, Figure 8L, Figure 8—source data 1
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data presented in Figure 8L.

claims.claim: Optogenetic inhibition of PVN (OTergic) to the prelimbic cortex pathway significantly increased anxiety-like behavior in females.
claims.source: Optogenetic inhibition of PVN (OTergic) to the PrL pathway significantly increased anxiety-like behavior (males: t(10) = 3.051, p<0.05, Figure 8L, Figure 8—source data 1; females: t(10) = 5.875, p<0.01, Figure 8M, Figure 8—source data 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data presented in Figure 8M.

claims.claim: Preweaning paternal deprivation increased anxiety-like behavior in mandarin voles in adulthood.
claims.source: The present study found that preweaning PD in mandarin vole pups increased the levels of anxiety-like behavior and attenuated social preference in male and female adults, possibly via disruption of emotional attachment.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from open field tests and light-dark tests.

claims.claim: Preweaning paternal deprivation attenuated social preference in mandarin voles in adulthood.
claims.source: The present study found that preweaning PD in mandarin vole pups increased the levels of anxiety-like behavior and attenuated social preference in male and female adults, possibly via disruption of emotional attachment.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from social preference tests.

claims.claim: Paternal deprivation decreased the neuronal activity in the prelimbic cortex during the social approach test.
claims.source: PD decreased the neuronal activity in the PrL and NAc shells and reduced the percentage of c-fos/OT-labeled cells in the PVN during the social approach test.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by c-fos immunohistochemistry data.

claims.claim: Paternal deprivation decreased the neuronal activity in the NAc shells during the social approach test.
claims.source: PD decreased the neuronal activity in the PrL and NAc shells and reduced the percentage of c-fos/OT-labeled cells in the PVN during the social approach test.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by c-fos immunohistochemistry data.

claims.claim: Paternal deprivation reduced the percentage of c-fos/OT-labeled cells in the PVN during the social approach test.
claims.source: PD decreased the neuronal activity in the PrL and NAc shells and reduced the percentage of c-fos/OT-labeled cells in the PVN during the social approach test.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by double-immunohistochemistry data for c-fos and OT.

claims.claim: Paternal deprivation reduced the number of PVN OT-IR neurons.
claims.source: PD also reduced the number of PVN OT-IR neurons and decreased the amounts of mPFC OTR protein in females and the OTR and V1aR proteins in males.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data for OT in the PVN.

claims.claim: Paternal deprivation decreased the amounts of medial prefrontal cortex oxytocin receptor protein in females.
claims.source: PD also reduced the number of PVN OT-IR neurons and decreased the amounts of mPFC OTR protein in females and the OTR and V1aR proteins in males.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Western blotting data for OTR in the mPFC.

claims.claim: Paternal deprivation decreased the amounts of medial prefrontal cortex oxytocin receptor protein in males.
claims.source: PD also reduced the number of PVN OT-IR neurons and decreased the amounts of mPFC OTR protein in females and the OTR and V1aR proteins in males.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Western blotting data for OTR in the mPFC.

claims.claim: Paternal deprivation decreased the amounts of medial prefrontal cortex V1aR protein in males.
claims.source: PD also reduced the number of PVN OT-IR neurons and decreased the amounts of mPFC OTR protein in females and the OTR and V1aR proteins in males.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Western blotting data for V1aR in the mPFC.

claims.claim: An intra-prelimbic cortical oxytocin injection restored the anxiety-like behavior altered by preweaning paternal deprivation.
claims.source: We then demonstrated that an intra-PrL OT injection restored the anxiety-like behavior and social preference altered by preweaning PD.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data from open field tests following OT microinjection.

claims.claim: An intra-prelimbic cortical oxytocin injection restored the social preference altered by preweaning paternal deprivation.
claims.source: We then demonstrated that an intra-PrL OT injection restored the anxiety-like behavior and social preference altered by preweaning PD.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data from social preference tests following OT microinjection.

claims.claim: Optogenetic activation of the PVN-PrL oxytocin terminals reduced anxiety-like behavior in paternal deprivation mandarin voles.
claims.source: For the first time, we showed that optogenetic activation of the PVN-PrL OT terminals reduced anxiety-like behavior and increased social-preference behavior in PD mandarin voles.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data from open field tests following optogenetic activation.

claims.claim: Optogenetic activation of the PVN-PrL oxytocin terminals increased social-preference behavior in paternal deprivation mandarin voles.
claims.source: For the first time, we showed that optogenetic activation of the PVN-PrL OT terminals reduced anxiety-like behavior and increased social-preference behavior in PD mandarin voles.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data from social preference tests following optogenetic activation.

claims.claim: Optogenetic inhibition of prelimbic cortex-projecting PVN OTergic neurons elicited anxiety-like behavior in naive mandarin voles.
claims.source: Optogenetic inhibition of PrL-projecting PVN OTergic neurons elicited anxiety-like behavior and decreased social preference in naive mandarin voles.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data from open field tests following optogenetic inhibition.

claims.claim: Optogenetic inhibition of prelimbic cortex-projecting PVN OTergic neurons decreased social preference in naive mandarin voles.
claims.source: Optogenetic inhibition of PrL-projecting PVN OTergic neurons elicited anxiety-like behavior and decreased social preference in naive mandarin voles.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data from social preference tests following optogenetic inhibition.

claims.claim: Offspring that experience neonatal maternal separation or early deprivation display high levels of anxiety-like behavior.
claims.source: It has previously been shown that offspring that experience neonatal maternal separation or early deprivation display high levels of anxiety-like behavior (Sachs et al., 2013; Wei et al., 2010; Koe et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Sachs et al., 2013; Wei et al., 2010; Koe et al., 2016.

claims.claim: Neonatal adversity induces changes in social behavior, including avoidance, fear and decreased social interactions.
claims.source: Neonatal adversity has been shown to induce changes in social behavior, including avoidance, fear and decreased social interactions (Giachino et al., 2007; Jia et al., 2009; Toth and Neumann, 2013).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Giachino et al., 2007; Jia et al., 2009; Toth and Neumann, 2013.

claims.claim: The medial prefrontal cortex may receive long-range axonal projections from oxytocin-producing neurons.
claims.source: The mPFC may receive long-range axonal projections from OT-producing neurons (Knobloch et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Knobloch et al., 2012.

claims.claim: Oxytocin in the prelimbic region of the medial prefrontal cortex decreased anxiety regardless of sex.
claims.source: A previous study found that OT in the PrL region of the mPFC decreased anxiety regardless of sex and that neither AVP nor OTR-A affected anxiety-like behavior (Sabihi et al., 2014b).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Sabihi et al., 2014b.

claims.claim: Blocking oxytocin receptor in the prelimbic cortex enhances postpartum anxiety but has no effect on anxiety in virgin females.
claims.source: Blocking OTR in the PrL enhances postpartum anxiety but has no effect on anxiety in virgin females (Sabihi et al., 2014a).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Sabihi et al., 2014a.

claims.claim: Oxytocin receptor knockout mice display deficits in social-approach behavior.
claims.source: OTR knockout mice display deﬁcits in social-approach behavior (Nishimori et al., 2008) and social memory (Lee et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Nishimori et al., 2008.

claims.claim: Oxytocin receptor knockout mice display deficits in social memory.
claims.source: OTR knockout mice display deﬁcits in social-approach behavior (Nishimori et al., 2008) and social memory (Lee et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lee et al., 2008.

claims.claim: PVN oxytocin neurons predominantly express vesicular glutamate transporter 2.
claims.source: PVN OT neurons predominantly express vesicular glutamate transporter 2, suggesting that depolarization of these neurons is coupled with synaptic glutamate release in their projections, such as those to the mPFC (Kawasaki et al., 2005; Johnson and Young, 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kawasaki et al., 2005; Johnson and Young, 2017.

claims.claim: Depolarization of PVN oxytocin neurons is coupled with synaptic glutamate release in their projections to the medial prefrontal cortex.
claims.source: PVN OT neurons predominantly express vesicular glutamate transporter 2, suggesting that depolarization of these neurons is coupled with synaptic glutamate release in their projections, such as those to the mPFC (Kawasaki et al., 2005; Johnson and Young, 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the expression of vesicular glutamate transporter 2 in PVN OT neurons, as supported by citations to Kawasaki et al., 2005; Johnson and Young, 2017.

claims.claim: A specific class of interneurons (OxtrINs) in the medial prefrontal cortex is critical for the modulation of social and emotional behaviors in both sexes.
claims.source: In addition, a specific class of interneurons (OxtrINs) in the mPFC is critical for the modulation of social and emotional behaviors in both sexes (Li et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Li et al., 2016.

claims.claim: Female prairie voles have greater densities of oxytocin receptor binding but lower densities of vasopressin 1a receptor binding than males in the medial prefrontal cortex.
claims.source: Female prairie voles have greater densities of OTR binding but lower densities of V1aR binding than males in the mPFC (Smeltzer et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Smeltzer et al., 2006.

claims.claim: Intracerebroventricular injections of oxytocin induce social communication by activating vasopressin 1a receptor in male Syrian hamsters.
claims.source: Intracerebroventricular (ICV) injections of OT induce social communication by activating V1aR in male Syrian hamsters (Song et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Song et al., 2014.

claims.claim: Some of the prosocial effects of oxytocin may be mediated by vasopressin 1a receptor in males.
claims.source: Studies have shown that some of the prosocial effects of OT may be mediated by V1aR in males (Sala et al., 2011; Ramos et al., 2013)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Sala et al., 2011; Ramos et al., 2013.

claims.claim: Vasopressin 1a receptor knockout mice have impaired social interactions.
claims.source: and that V1aR knockout mice have impaired social interactions (Egashira et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Egashira et al., 2007.

claims.claim: Paternal deprivation from weaning to adolescence decreased the number of oxytocin-positive neurons in the PVN of mandarin voles.
claims.source: Consistent with previous reports, PD from weaning (Feng et al., 2019) to adolescence (Wang et al., 2017) decreased the number of OT-positive neurons in the PVN of mandarin voles.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Feng et al., 2019 and Wang et al., 2017.

claims.claim: Maternal separation decreases the number of PVN oxytocin-IR neurons in females but not in males.
claims.source: Maternal separation is known to decrease the number of PVN OT-IR neurons in females but not in males (Veenema et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Veenema et al., 2007.

claims.claim: Social approach was improved by activating endogenous oxytocin neurons in the PVN with chemogenetics.
claims.source: Previous studies found that social approach (Peñagarikano et al., 2015) and mood (Grund et al., 2017) were improved by activating endogenous oxytocin neurons in the PVN with chemogenetics.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Peñagarikano et al., 2015.

claims.claim: Mood was improved by activating endogenous oxytocin neurons in the PVN with chemogenetics.
claims.source: Previous studies found that social approach (Peñagarikano et al., 2015) and mood (Grund et al., 2017) were improved by activating endogenous oxytocin neurons in the PVN with chemogenetics.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Grund et al., 2017.

claims.claim: Oxytocin infusion into the prelimbic cortex reverses amphetamine-induced deficits in social bonding.

results.result: Preweaning paternal deprivation (PND 14-21) increased anxiety-like behavior in both male and female mandarin voles, as measured by reduced time in the central area of the open field test and reduced time in the light compartment of the light-dark test.
results.evaluation: Claims C33, C34, C37, and C38 provide converging evidence from two independent behavioral assays (open field and light-dark tests) showing increased anxiety-like behavior in both sexes following paternal deprivation. Statistical significance is reported for all comparisons (p<0.01 or p<0.05), and the results are consistent across tests and sexes.

results.result: Paternal deprivation did not affect locomotor activity (total distance traveled) in the open field test in either sex.
results.evaluation: Claims C35 and C36 demonstrate that the anxiety-like behavioral changes were not confounded by alterations in general locomotor activity, strengthening the interpretation that the effects are specific to anxiety rather than motor function.

results.result: Preweaning paternal deprivation reduced social preference in male mandarin voles but had less clear effects in females, with biparental care males showing preference for social over object stimuli while paternal deprivation males did not.
results.evaluation: Claims C39, C40, and C41 show that PC males preferred social stimuli (p<0.025) while PD males did not, indicating impaired social preference. In females, the main effect of stimulus was significant but the treatment effect was not, suggesting a more subtle or variable effect. The sex difference in response is notable.

results.result: Paternal deprivation reduced the activation of PVN oxytocin neurons during social approach, particularly in females, as measured by c-fos/OT double-labeling.
results.evaluation: Claims C42, C43, and C44 demonstrate that PC voles showed increased c-fos/OT labeling when approaching juvenile voles versus toys (p<0.01 in both sexes), while PD voles did not show this differential activation. The effect was statistically significant in females (p<0.01) but not males, suggesting sex-specific alterations in OT neuron responsiveness.

results.result: Paternal deprivation reduced neuronal activity (c-fos expression) in the prelimbic cortex during social approach in both sexes.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C48 show that PC voles had more c-fos-positive neurons after exposure to juvenile voles versus toys (p<0.01 in both sexes), while PD voles showed reduced c-fos expression compared to PC voles (p<0.01 in both sexes). This indicates impaired PrL activation during social encounters following paternal deprivation.

results.result: Paternal deprivation altered c-fos expression in the nucleus accumbens shell in a sex-specific manner during social approach.
results.evaluation: Claims C49 and C50 demonstrate sex-specific effects: PD males showed decreased c-fos in NAc shell after juvenile vole exposure (p<0.05), while PC females showed fewer c-fos-positive nuclei after approaching juvenile voles versus toys (p<0.01), an effect absent in PD females. This suggests sex-dependent alterations in reward circuitry.

results.result: Paternal deprivation reduced the number of oxytocin-immunoreactive neurons in the PVN in both sexes, with females having more OT-IR neurons than males overall.
results.evaluation: Claims C51 and C52 show that PD reduced PVN OT-IR neurons in both sexes (p<0.01) and that females had more OT-IR neurons than males (p<0.01). The statistical analysis (two-way ANOVA with significant interaction) and post-hoc tests support these conclusions. However, sample size is small (n=4 per group).

results.result: Paternal deprivation decreased oxytocin receptor protein levels in the medial prefrontal cortex in both sexes, and decreased V1aR protein levels in males only.
results.evaluation: Claims C53, C54, and C55 demonstrate sex-specific effects on receptor expression: both sexes showed reduced mPFC OTR (males p<0.01, females p<0.01), while only males showed reduced V1aR (p<0.05). Western blotting data support these findings, though sample sizes are modest (n=6 per group).

results.result: Microinjection of oxytocin into the prelimbic cortex rescued anxiety-like behavior and social preference deficits induced by paternal deprivation in both sexes.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C59 show that intra-PrL OT increased time in central area (p<0.05) and restored social preference (p<0.008) in PD voles. The effects were blocked by OTR antagonist (except in one male dose group), demonstrating receptor specificity. This is a key pharmacological rescue experiment supporting the role of PrL OT signaling.

results.result: Optogenetic activation of PVN oxytocin neuron terminals in the prelimbic cortex rescued anxiety-like behavior and social preference deficits in paternal deprivation voles.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C66 demonstrate that ChR2-expressing neurons colocalized with OT neurons (60.6% males, 70.9% females), optogenetic activation increased PrL c-fos (p<0.01), and rescued both anxiety (p<0.01) and social preference behaviors (p<0.025). This circuit-specific manipulation provides strong causal evidence for the PVN-PrL OT pathway's role. However, colocalization percentages indicate incomplete specificity.

results.result: Optogenetic inhibition of PVN oxytocin neuron terminals in the prelimbic cortex induced anxiety-like behavior and reduced social preference in naive voles.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C75 show that eNpHR3.0 neurons colocalized with OT neurons (70.1% males, 77.6% females), optogenetic inhibition decreased PrL c-fos (p<0.01), and induced anxiety (males p<0.05, females p<0.01) and reduced social preference in naive voles. This loss-of-function experiment complements the gain-of-function results, though the social preference effect in males was less robust.

results.result: Preweaning paternal deprivation produces long-lasting alterations in anxiety-like behavior, social preference, and the oxytocin system, including reduced OT neuron numbers, decreased OT/c-fos activation, and reduced OTR/V1aR protein levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C84 summarize the main findings showing that PD (PND 14-21) produces persistent effects measured at PND 70. The convergence of behavioral, immunohistochemical, and Western blotting data provides strong support. However, these are summary claims that aggregate the specific experimental results already evaluated above.

results.result: Both pharmacological (OT microinjection) and optogenetic (ChR2 activation) interventions targeting the PrL rescued PD-induced behavioral deficits, while optogenetic inhibition (eNpHR3.0) of the PVN-PrL OT pathway mimicked PD effects in naive animals.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C90 summarize the intervention experiments. The bidirectional optogenetic manipulations (activation rescues deficits, inhibition induces deficits) combined with pharmacological rescue provide strong causal evidence for the PVN-PrL OT pathway's role. These summary claims are well-supported by the specific experimental results.

results.result: The PVN-PrL oxytocin pathway mediates the effects of early paternal deprivation on anxiety and social behavior, with sex-specific modulation, and represents a potential therapeutic target.
results.evaluation: Claims C126-C129 represent the main conclusions of the study. The convergence of behavioral, molecular, pharmacological, and optogenetic evidence supports the central role of the PVN-PrL OT pathway. Sex differences are documented in receptor expression and some behavioral responses. However, C129's therapeutic potential claim is speculative and would require additional validation studies.

results.result: Paternal deprivation has significant negative effects on child development in humans and impairs various social and emotional behaviors in rodent models.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C9 provide background context from prior literature. These are citation-based claims establishing the rationale for the study. While the citations support the claims, the accuracy depends on the cited sources, which cannot be independently verified here. These are standard literature review claims.

results.result: Mandarin voles are socially monogamous with biparental care, and pups show high attachment to fathers during PND 14-21, making them a suitable model for studying paternal deprivation effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C10-C18 establish the biological characteristics of the mandarin vole model and justify the PND 14-21 deprivation period. These are primarily citation-based claims (C10-C12, C17-C18) with some observational claims (C13, C15-C16). The model justification is reasonable, though C14 is an inference about thermoregulation from fur development.

results.result: The oxytocin system, particularly in the medial prefrontal cortex and its subregions, plays critical roles in social behavior and anxiety regulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C32 provide extensive background on the OT system and mPFC function from prior literature. These citation-based claims establish the neurobiological framework for the study's hypotheses. The claims are well-supported by multiple citations, though their accuracy depends on the cited sources.

results.result: Prior research demonstrates that early life stress affects the oxytocin system, that OT neurons project from PVN to mPFC and NAc, and that OT signaling in these regions regulates social and emotional behaviors.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C125 provide extensive literature review establishing: (1) effects of early adversity on OT system, (2) anatomical projections of OT neurons, (3) functional roles of OT in behavior, and (4) interactions with other neurotransmitter systems. These citation-based claims provide comprehensive background but are not primary findings of this study.
